newsitem.title: USA: American Air to buy 103 Boeing planes.
newsitem.headline: American Air to buy 103 Boeing planes.

text.p: American Airlines announced a major overhaul of its fleet Thursday, pledging to buy 103 jets from Boeing Co. and taking options on 527 more in one of the biggest commercial airplane orders in history.
Marking a huge victory for the world's largest aircraft manufacturer, Dallas-based American Airlines said Boeing would be its exclusive provider through the year 2018.

Based on list prices, the 103-plane purchase is worth about $6.5 billion, and the entire package could be worth more than $35 billion, though Robert Crandall, chairman of American parent company AMR Corp.., said wryly that he got a good discount from the list prices.
American, the nation's second-largest airline, said it will accept delivery of the 103 aircraft over four years starting in 1998.

The order consists of models ranging from Boeing 737s to 777s, with the bulk of the order and options consisting of 737s. The 737s, the world's most popular jetliners, seat from 108 to 189 passengers.

Crandall said the 75 Boeing 737s under firm order would replace American's ageing fleet of 727s, while 12 new wide-body 777s will take the place of its McDonnell Douglas Corp.-built MD-11s, which American executives have not been impressed by.

The American-Boeing deal is another slap in the face for McDonnell Douglas. It has said it will be no more than a niche player in the commercial aircraft market and last week was knocked out of contention for a new fighter plane, the Pentagon's biggest weapons programme of the early 21st century.
Crandall said he did not even consider McDonnell Douglas' 90/95 family of jets as American looked to update its fleet, dismissing them as "obsolete technology."
Now that the deal with Seattle-based Boeing is in place, Crandall said American plans to phase out its 260 MD-80s and 75 Fokker NV 100 planes over the next 20 years.
Of the 527 Boeing planes on option, 425 are 737s.
"There are huge advantages in having our fleet made up of jets from the same family," Crandall said, pointing to lower costs of maintenance, repairs and training.

The newer jets were also more fuel-efficient and less polluting than those they will replace. But Crandall also said American has been pleased with its 35 Airbus A300 planes and expects them to fly through their full life cycle.
Despite the huge dollar value of the deal, it represents more a modernisation than a rapid expansion of American's fleet, which currently stands at 640 planes.
Crandall said he expects it to bring a capacity increase of between 1.5 percent and 2.0 percent per year over the next five years.

"Two percent growth is entirely consistent with the rate at which the market will grow. It will allow us to remain competitive and, hopefully, profitable as well," he said. "We do not went to grow very rapidly, but we do want the ability to grow in those markets where we do best."

The new 777s fit in well with American's plans to expand its trans-Pacific routes to Tokyo and further into Asia. The growth prospects of those Asian markets and of the carrier's Latin American services are widely seen as more dynamic than those for its domestic operations.

Crandall also stressed American has no firm commitment to buying a single one of the 527 Boeing planes it has options on. Exactly how many it takes will depend on market conditions in what is a notoriously cyclical industry, he said.

The deal is also contingent on ratification of a tentative labour pact between American and the Allied Pilots Association, whose 9,150 members will vote on the agreement in December. The association's board on Wednesday voted 10-8 to accept the pact and union members were expected to back it.
American plans to sell most of its MD-11s to Federal Express Corp.
Boeing stock added $1.125 to $97.50, AMR lost 50 cents to $90.50 and McDonnell Douglas fell 12.5 cents to $53, all on the New York Stock Exchange.
